newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb politician critical after suicide bid.
newsitem.headline: Serb politician critical after suicide bid.

text.p: Former Bosnian Serb vice-president Nikola Koljevic shot himself in the head in a suicide attempt and was on Friday in a critical condition at a Belgrade hospital, officials said.

Koljevic, 60, a Shakespeare scholar and former Sarajevo university professor, was in a coma after "tragic self-inflicted wounds", a statement issued by Dragan Kalinic, speaker of the Bosnian Serb republic's assembly in the town of Pale, said.
Hospital doctors had taken all possible measures "to improve the patient's condition and maintain his vital functions", Kalinic's statement said.
Political sources said Koljevic shot himself on Thursday night in his office in Pale, a mountain village near Sarajevo.
He was evacuated by helicopter on Friday to Belgrade, capital of neighbouring Serbia, in a French helicopter provided by the NATO-led peacekeeping force in Bosnia.
Reporters saw Serb security officers and NATO soldiers carry Koljevic on a stretcher to the French Puma helicopter at about 3 p.m. near a hospital in Sokolac, 30 km (18 miles) from Pale.
Heavy fog in Sarajevo and Belgrade had prevented evacuating Koljevic earlier in the day, doctors and NATO officers said.
Koljevic was admitted to the Yugoslav army's medical academy hospital (VMA) where doctors began emergency surgery.

"The head of neuro-surgery, who is just now performing surgery with his team, has described Dr Koljevic's condition as extremely undertain and hence still critical," Colonel Radoslav Svicevic, a VMA spokesman, said late on Friday afternoon.
Few details of the reported suicide were available and the Bosnian Serb police had yet to issue any official account.
Political sources said Koljevic, who lives in Belgrade, arrived in Pale with his wife at about midday on Thursday and later picked up passport-sized photos at a shop.
He took a walk with his wife in the afternoon and went alone to his office building where other Serb politicians work, the sources said.
He was later found bleeding in a small bedroom above his office by police. The sources alleged police had to break the door open because it was locked.
It remained unclear whether Koljevic suffered one or two gunshot wounds, the sources said.
Koljevic played a prominent public role in the Serb leadership during the Bosnian war but was pushed aside after the signing of the Dayton peace agreement in November 1995.
He started to fade from view in 1994 and turned his attention to writing and editing.

Koljevic belonged to Bosnia's ill-fated collective presidency when war erupted in May 1992, and was a member of the ultra-nationalist Serb Democratic Party led by Radovan Karadzic, now an indicted war criminal.

He often struck a more moderate tone than other Serb leaders when speaking to reporters or foreign envoys. Karadzic assigned Koljevic the task of reassuring international relief officials who drove up to Pale pleading for safe passage for aid convoys.

At the close of the war Koljevic, unlike other hardline Serb officials, chose to cooperate with Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, who forced his proteges in Bosnia to accept the Dayton peace agreement.
